scope: Which object IDs a store read may request from the object-job port, and how a request the server partly rejects is split. Measured on Git 2.50.1 in explorations/repository-cache/results/gitlinks.json.

change_set.listing: git diff --raw -z --no-abbrev --no-renames <left> <right>, run with GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1 and the store read configuration; both sides of every entry are considered and the all-zero object ID is ignored.
rules: Only blob modes are requested. A tree never appears without -t and is present in a blobless store anyway.

A 160000 entry is a gitlink: its object ID names a commit in another repository. It is reported as a submodule entry, never requested, and never reported missing, even though cat-file --batch-check calls it missing.
An unknown mode is a typed unsupported_entry, never requested.

request.split: Try the whole list; if the server rejects it with a per-object rejection, split it into the first ceil(n/2) object IDs and the rest and retry each part, depth first; a rejected single object ID is marked unavailable individually.
request.terminal_rule: A terminal failure fails the whole job without splitting: splitting a list the server refuses as a policy would issue 2n - 1 requests for nothing. Failure text that matches no known class is unclassified and terminal, because only a recognized per-object rejection is evidence that splitting can succeed.
request.cap_rule: Once a job has marked rejected_leaf_cap object IDs unavailable, it issues no further requests; every object ID not yet accepted or rejected is marked deferred, not unavailable, so a later convergence retries it.
request.cap_reasoning: A provisional cost policy, not a performance bound: nothing was measured about how many rejections real servers produce. Blob-mode filtering removes the one routine cause measured (gitlinks), so more than a handful of rejected objects in one job suggests a force-pushed history or a server policy the split cannot fix, and eight keeps the worst case to a few hundred requests. Revisit it when rejection wording and frequency are measured on hosting providers.
request.request_bound: With r rejected object IDs among n, the split issues at most 1 + 2 * min(r, rejected_leaf_cap) * ceil(log2 n) requests; at the 50,000-ID request limit that is at most 1 + 2 * 8 * 16 = 257.
request.unmeasured: Rejection wording was measured only against a file:// origin (not our ref). GitHub wording is measured by the broker-pinned Git credential bridge (mb-s123) and GitLab wording by the GitLab adapter (mb-51uj); until then every other message from those hosts is unclassified and terminal.

request_cases.why: The measured flow: 11 blobs, one gitlink commit ID at position 4, and one object ID the origin does not have, against a file:// origin over protocol v2.
Measured with protocol v0 and no uploadpack.allowAnySHA1InWant: the server refused every unadvertised object, including blobs it has.
Ten of sixteen object IDs are rejected; after eight rejections the job stops and defers what it has not resolved.

job_sources.rule: A fetch job names a remote recorded in the store's configuration snapshot, never a URL. For a blobless store that remote must also be recorded as a promisor. The job's destination refs are private to the job. Provider change-request heads are fetched from the base repository's provider-published refs through the store's own remote; an object reachable only from a fork is acquired through the fork's own source and store.
job_sources.basis: Measured on Git 2.50.1 (results/storeconfig.json): fetching a fork by URL into a blobless store with the filter wrote remote.<url>.promisor and remote.<url>.partialclonefilter into the store's configuration; without the filter it wrote objects that made gc --prune=now fail with Packfile doesn't have full closure. Fetching the same commit through the base repository's refs/pull/1/head and the store's own remote left the configuration unchanged and gc and repack succeeded.
